title: On the spin dependence of the emergent gravity phenomena as observed in axially symmetric black hole accretion with spatially varying adiabatic index
comment: 24 pages, Revtex class, 10 figures (original abstract differes slightly)
summary: The present work addresses an axisymmetrically accreting black hole system from three perspectives: the astrophysical, the dynamical systems, and the emergent gravity standpoint. Steady-state equations governing low angular momentum axially symmetric accretion under a pseudo-Kerr potential are formulated for a multi-species flow with a spatially varying adiabatic index. The resulting transonic solutions are shown to be multi-transonic and may accommodate a stationary shock. Critical points are classified via perturbative dynamical systems methods, and linear stability analysis confirms that the stationary solutions remain stable under radial perturbation. The ensuing acoustic geometry harbours acoustic black holes at the sonic points and an acoustic white hole at the shock location, whose causal structure is constructed via the Carter--Penrose diagram. The surface gravity associated with each acoustic horizon is computed using a generalized expression that accounts for the spatial variation of the local sound speed.

AI.tldr: This paper studies axisymmetric black hole accretion using a pseudo-Kerr potential, analyzing multi-species transonic flows with variable adiabatic index. It identifies multi-transonic solutions with possible stationary shocks, classifies critical points via dynamical systems, confirms stability, and finds acoustic black/white holes with computed surface gravity.
AI.motivation: To bridge astrophysical accretion theory, dynamical systems analysis, and emergent gravity by studying low angular momentum accretion onto a black hole in a pseudo-Kerr framework with a spatially varying adiabatic index.
AI.method: Steady-state equations are formulated for axisymmetric multi-species flow under a pseudo-Kerr potential. Critical points are classified via perturbative dynamical systems methods; linear stability analysis is performed; acoustic geometry is analyzed via Carter-Penrose diagrams; surface gravity is computed with a generalized expression accounting for variable sound speed.
AI.result: Solutions are multi-transonic and can accommodate stationary shocks. Critical point classification is achieved, stationary solutions are linearly stable under radial perturbation. Acoustic black holes form at sonic points and an acoustic white hole at the shock location; surface gravity is generalized for variable sound speed.
AI.conclusion: The multi-species, variable-adiabatic-index accretion model exhibits rich transonic behavior and acoustic spacetime structures, offering a unified perspective across astrophysics, dynamical systems, and emergent gravity.

title: Multiwavelength Characterization of a New Magnetic Cataclysmic Variable 2CXO J050740.7-091337
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Published in PASP
summary: We report the discovery and characterization of a new cataclysmic variable (CV), 2CXO J050740.7-091337 (hereafter 2CXO J0507), identified using the X-ray main sequence through a cross-match between the Chandra Source Catalogue 2.1 and Gaia DR3. Optical spectroscopic follow-up with Keck I/LRIS reveals prominent cyclotron humps and Balmer emission lines, indicating a strongly magnetized white dwarf with a magnetic field strength of $B \approx 30$ MG. Analysis of Chandra and XMM-Newton archival data shows an X-ray luminosity of $L_X = (5.18 \pm 0.88) \times 10^{30}$ erg s$^{-1}$ (0.3-10 keV). The X-ray spectrum is well approximated by a thermal plasma emission model with a temperature of $kT = 7.95^{+3.84}_{-1.85}$ keV, showing no soft excess or intrinsic absorption. 2CXO J0507 exhibits long-term optical variability by $\approx2$ mag (ranging $\approx18-20$ mag) in Zwicky Transient Facility and Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System photometric data. Both X-ray and optical modulation suggest an orbital period of 2.34 hr. These properties indicate that 2CXO J0507 is a magnetic CV, most closely resembling a polar. As 2CXO J0507 sits close to the faint limit of current optical time-domain surveys, it serves as a representative example of the large population of faint, magnetic CVs expected to be systematically identified by the Rubin Observatory.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the discovery of 2CXO J050740.7-091337, a magnetic cataclysmic variable (polar) with a ~30 MG white dwarf, identified via cross-matching Chandra and Gaia data, with an orbital period of 2.34 hr and X-ray luminosity of ~5×10³⁰ erg s⁻¹.
AI.motivation: To identify and characterize faint, magnetic cataclysmic variables in the X-ray main sequence that are difficult to detect with current optical surveys, leveraging high-energy catalog cross-matching to uncover hidden populations.
AI.method: Cross-match between Chandra Source Catalogue 2.1 and Gaia DR3; optical spectroscopy with Keck I/LRIS; X-ray spectral and timing analysis of Chandra and XMM-Newton archival data; optical light curve analysis from ZTF and ATLAS.
AI.result: Discovered magnetic CV with B ≈ 30 MG, L_X = (5.18 ± 0.88) × 10³⁰ erg s⁻¹, X-ray plasma temperature kT = 7.95^{+3.84}_{-1.85} keV, orbital period of 2.34 hr, and ~2 mag optical variability.
AI.conclusion: 2CXO J0507 is a polar-type magnetic CV near the faint limit of current surveys; it exemplifies the large undiscovered population of faint magnetic CVs that the Rubin Observatory will systematically identify.

title: Sensitivity of the As-Built Askaryan Radio Array to Ultra-High Energy Neutrinos
summary: The Askaryan Radio Array (ARA) is an ultra-high energy (UHE) neutrino observatory designed to detect the impulsive radio waves produced by relativistic particle cascades in the Antarctic glacial ice. Using a significantly enhanced simulation pipeline, which adds data-driven detector simulations and fully incorporates secondary particle production, we calculate the trigger-level acceptance of the entire array. We compare the resulting trigger-level sensitivity to constraints on the UHE neutrino flux from other detectors. Given its exposure from 2013 to 2023, we find that ARA achieves a world-leading sensitivity above about $10^{19}$ eV, depending on the details of the event selection used in a search. Moreover, we find that up to 13 neutrinos are predicted to have been observed in this period at trigger-level, assuming the most optimistic neutrino flux models. We show that observations of secondary particles account for up to 30\% of the total acceptance starting at $10^{19}$ eV, and we explore the potential signatures and implications of both multi-pulse (from direct and refracted pulses and/or from secondary particle interactions) and multi-station events. Finally, we comment on the implications of this study for the design of next-generation UHE neutrino experiments, in particular IceCube-Gen2 Radio.

AI.tldr: The ARA neutrino observatory achieves world-leading sensitivity above ~10^19 eV using an enhanced simulation pipeline that incorporates data-driven detector simulations and secondary particle production. Up to 13 neutrinos may have been observed at trigger-level under optimistic models, with secondary particles contributing up to 30% of acceptance. Findings inform next-generation experiments like IceCube-Gen2 Radio.
AI.motivation: To improve the understanding of ARA's trigger-level acceptance and sensitivity for ultra-high energy neutrinos by incorporating more realistic simulations including secondary particle production and data-driven detector effects.
AI.method: Developed a significantly enhanced simulation pipeline that adds data-driven detector simulations and fully incorporates secondary particle production to calculate the trigger-level acceptance across the entire ARA array.
AI.result: ARA achieves world-leading sensitivity above ~10^19 eV based on 2013-2023 exposure. Up to 13 neutrinos may have been observed at trigger-level under optimistic flux models. Secondary particles account for up to 30% of total acceptance above 10^19 eV. Both multi-pulse and multi-station events are identified as potential signatures.
AI.conclusion: The study provides implications for next-generation UHE neutrino experiments, particularly IceCube-Gen2 Radio, by demonstrating the importance of secondary particle contributions and multi-pulse/station signatures for future detector design.

title: HD3191, the high-mass X-ray binary that wasn't there
comment: Accepted for publication in New Astronomy
summary: The rapidly rotating B1 IV:nn star HD3191 lies within the error box of a flaring Fermi gamma-ray source. Although the counterpart of the Fermi source is likely an active galaxy, HD3191 has nevertheless been suggested to be a high-mass X-ray binary, possibly hosting a black hole companion. The star displays roughly sinusoidal photometric variations with amplitudes of about 12 mmag for two frequencies $ν_1$ = 0.1235 d$^{-1}$ and $ν_2$ = 1.6038 d$^{-1}$. Half of the former frequency ($ν_1$/2) had previously been interpreted as the orbital frequency of a high-mass X-ray binary in which the B1 IV:nn primary undergoes ellipsoidal variations. We show that this scenario fails to account for the lack of significant radial velocity variations and for the overall properties of the star. Our spectroscopic observations instead unveil line profile variations, suggesting that the photometric and line profile variations arise from multi-mode pulsations rather than from orbital effects. Whilst we cannot rule out the possibility that HD3191 could be a nascent binary, consisting of a B1 IV:nn with a low-mass pre-main sequence companion, the most likely scenario is a single star displaying non-radial pulsations. The fast stellar rotation would thus be intrinsic to the B1 IV:nn star rather than being the result of a spin-up during a past mass-transfer episode.

AI.tldr: This paper re-examines the B1 IV:nn star HD3191, previously suggested to be a high-mass X-ray binary with a black hole companion based on photometric variations interpreted as ellipsoidal modulations. Using spectroscopic observations, the authors find line profile variations and the absence of radial velocity variations, concluding that the observed variability arises from multi-mode non-radial pulsations rather than orbital effects. The star is most likely a single, rapidly rotating pulsating star, not a binary.
AI.motivation: To test whether HD3191, a rapidly rotating B1 IV:nn star associated with a Fermi gamma-ray source, is a high-mass X-ray binary (HMXB) with a black hole companion as previously suggested, or if its photometric variations have an alternative explanation.
AI.method: Spectroscopic observations to measure radial velocity variations and analyze line profile variability, combined with re-analysis of existing photometric data showing two dominant frequencies (ν1 = 0.1235 d⁻¹ and ν2 = 1.6038 d⁻¹).
AI.result: No significant radial velocity variations were found, contrary to expectations for an HMXB. Line profile variations were detected, consistent with non-radial pulsations. The previously interpreted orbital frequency (ν1/2) does not hold up under scrutiny.
AI.conclusion: HD3191 is most likely a single star exhibiting multi-mode non-radial pulsations; the fast rotation is intrinsic rather than from past mass transfer. A low-mass pre-main sequence companion cannot be entirely ruled out but is unlikely.

title: Galactic Amnesia: The Information Washout of the Milky Way Merger History
comment: 29 + 7 pages, 14 + 4 figures, to be submitted to ApJ
summary: The merger history of a galaxy leaves imprints on its present-day stellar chemodynamics, yet dynamical processes progressively erase this record. We ask: how far back in time, and from which observables, can a galaxy's assembly history still be recovered? We provide a quantitative framework to address this question, using Mutual Information normalized by Shannon entropy to measure how much present-day stellar chemodynamics retains about each past merger's stellar mass $M_\star$ and infall time $t_{\rm infall}$. This framework is applied to TNG50 Milky Way -- like galaxies, with comparison to FIRE-2. We find that the gravitational potential and total energy are the most informative and longest-lived tracers of merger properties, highlighting the need for accurately measuring the Milky Way's potential. The information carried by the radial velocity decays to the noise floor within $\sim$5 Gyr, angular momentum carries low information overall with a mass-dependent decay, and chemical abundances retain a flat, low information floor. Information washout depends on three key factors: (1) radial position -- stars in the inner galaxy lose information faster due to shorter orbital times; (2) infall time -- old mergers are largely phase-mixed; and (3) merger mass -- larger mergers sink to the bottom of the potential well via dynamical friction, inducing violent relaxation that erases dynamical information. At each galactocentric radius, we map the observational horizon in the $(M_\star,\; t_{\rm infall})$ plane beyond which past mergers can no longer be recovered from that observable. By recasting merger reconstruction into this quantitative, observable-by-observable map of what is and is not recoverable, our results provide a foundation for interpreting chemodynamical signatures of past mergers and for guiding surveys and modeling toward the observables that maximize merger information recovery.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies how far back a galaxy's merger history can be recovered from present-day stellar chemodynamics using mutual information normalized by Shannon entropy, applied to TNG50 and FIRE-2 simulations. Gravitational potential and total energy are the most informative and longest-lived tracers; radial velocity information decays within ~5 Gyr; angular momentum shows mass-dependent decay; chemical abundances carry low information. Information washout depends on radial position, infall time, and merger mass. The study provides observational horizon maps in the (M★, tinfall) plane per observable.
AI.motivation: To quantitatively determine how far back in time and from which observables a galaxy's assembly history can still be recovered, given that dynamical processes progressively erase chemodynamical imprints of past mergers.
AI.method: Used Mutual Information normalized by Shannon entropy to measure how much present-day stellar chemodynamics retains about past merger properties (stellar mass M★ and infall time tinfall). Applied to TNG50 Milky Way-like galaxies with comparison to FIRE-2 simulations.
AI.result: Gravitational potential and total energy are the most informative and longest-lived tracers. Radial velocity information decays to noise floor within ~5 Gyr. Angular momentum carries low information with mass-dependent decay. Chemical abundances retain a flat, low information floor. Information washout depends on radial position, infall time, and merger mass.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a quantitative framework and observational horizon maps per observable for merger reconstruction, highlighting the need for accurate Milky Way potential measurements and guiding surveys toward observables that maximize merger information recovery.

title: Spectro-Polarimetric Observations of TeV Sources (SPOTS): First results
comment: 23 pages, 14 figures, 8 tables, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Blazars are jetted active galactic nuclei, with the jet aligned along the observer's line of sight. Their spectral energy distributions are dominated by non-thermal emission, with an underlying thermal component at optical/ultraviolet wavelengths. However, the underlying jet magnetic field structure and particle acceleration mechanisms requirements for the non-thermal emission are still under debate. Polarization measurements can provide critical insights, and we investigate the optical polarization properties of TeV-emitting blazars using long-term optical monitoring. We present results from the first 21-months of the Spectro-Polarimetric Observations of TeV Sources (SPOTS) campaign, using the Southern African Large Telescope, of 14 blazars. Overall, observations of the sample during this campaign showed a low average optical polarization ($Π\lesssim10\%$). While some sources exhibited smooth polarization angle rotations on timescales of days to weeks, others showed stochastic variations consistent with turbulent magnetic fields. The average ordering of the magnetic field was low ($F_B\lesssim0.10$), consistent with emission arising in extended, turbulent regions of the jet. For individual sources, correlations between polarization and its frequency dependence were found, but were not found across the entire sample. The nature of the frequency dependence varied between observations, indicating that simple one-zone models are insufficient and that $F_B$ must be wavelength dependent. This study highlights the complex nature of blazar jets and underscores the importance of long-term, multi-wavelength polarimetric monitoring. This comprehensive dataset enables detailed modelling of individual sources, and provides valuable context for future X-ray polarimetry observations.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes optical polarization data from 14 TeV-emitting blazars over 21 months (SPOTS campaign). Results show low average polarization (<10%), low magnetic field ordering (FB<0.10), and complex variability—smooth polarization angle rotations in some sources, stochastic turbulent behavior in others. Frequency dependence of polarization varied between observations, challenging simple one-zone emission models and highlighting the need for multi-wavelength polarimetric monitoring.
AI.motivation: The magnetic field structure and particle acceleration mechanisms in blazar jets remain debated. Polarization measurements offer critical constraints to understand these processes.
AI.method: Long-term optical spectropolarimetric monitoring of 14 TeV-emitting blazars over 21 months using the Southern African Large Telescope as part of the SPOTS campaign.
AI.result: Low average polarization (Π≲10%), low magnetic field ordering (FB≲0.10), smooth polarization angle rotations in some sources, stochastic variations in others, and observation-dependent frequency dependence of polarization.
AI.conclusion: Simple one-zone models are insufficient; magnetic field ordering is wavelength-dependent. Long-term, multi-wavelength polarimetric monitoring is essential for understanding blazar jet emission and for future X-ray polarimetry.

title: The galaxy-halo connection and the dynamical evolution of a giant disc in a massive node of the Cosmic Web at z~3
comment: 13 pages + 4 pages in the Appendix, 7 figures + 6 figures in the Appendix. Submitted to A&A
summary: Recent JWST observations revealed the surprising presence of a giant and massive disc galaxy in a Cosmic Web node at z$\sim3$. This galaxy, named the Big Wheel, has a size almost three times larger than expected for typical disc galaxies at the same redshift and similar stellar masses. Constraining the origin and formation history of the Big Wheel requires knowledge of its dark matter halo properties, which are difficult to derive from JWST observations alone. Here, we investigate the dark matter halo of the Big Wheel and provide further constraints on the galaxy baryonic content, combining a physically motivated dynamical model with deep ALMA kinematical data. By using priors based on JWST photometric data and CO kinematics, we infer a dark matter halo mass of $\log (M_{h}/M_{\odot})= 12.11^{+0.29}_{-0.17}$ and a stellar mass of $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})=11.00^{+0.11}_{-0.12}$, leading to a stellar-to-halo mass (SHM) ratio of $M_\star/M_h=0.06^{+0.04}_{-0.03}$. This value is significantly higher than expected from state-of-the-art empirical SHM relations. This implies that the Big Wheel may have assembled its stellar content in a much more efficient way with respect to the general galaxy population at z$\sim3$. Combined with its morphological properties, our results suggest that the Big Wheel had a tranquil recent formation history, with probably no major mergers, violent disc instabilities, or strong ejective feedback. We perform a numerical simulation of an idealised galaxy and let it evolve adiabatically for $2.5$ Gyr to demonstrate that it does not develop gravitational instabilities during its evolution that could alter its resemblance to the observed one. Although systems alike the Big Wheel are arguably rare, our results offer new constraints on the contribution of accretion and feedback to the formation history of the most massive discs within high-redshift Cosmic Web nodes.

AI.tldr: JWST and ALMA observations reveal the Big Wheel, a giant disc galaxy at z~3 in a Cosmic Web node, which has an unusually high stellar-to-halo mass ratio (0.06) and a tranquil formation history, implying highly efficient stellar assembly without major mergers or violent feedback.
AI.motivation: JWST discovered a surprisingly large disc galaxy (the Big Wheel) at z~3, whose origin is unclear because dark matter halo properties are difficult to derive from photometry alone.
AI.method: Combined physically motivated dynamical model with deep ALMA CO kinematics and JWST photometric priors to infer dark matter halo mass, stellar mass, and SHM ratio; also performed idealized numerical simulations of adiabatic evolution over 2.5 Gyr.
AI.result: Inferred log(M_h/M_sun)=12.11, log(M_star/M_sun)=11.00, SHM ratio=0.06 — significantly above empirical relations. Simulation shows no gravitational instabilities developing.
AI.conclusion: The Big Wheel assembled its stellar content more efficiently than typical z~3 galaxies, had a quiescent recent history with no major mergers or strong feedback, and offers constraints on accretion and feedback in massive discs within high-redshift Cosmic Web nodes.

title: Dynamics and Radiative Signatures of Accretion Flows onto a Kerr-like Wormhole
comment: 15pages, 13 figures; Accepted by Apj, comments wellcome
summary: Wormholes are a hypothetical object that connects disparate points in spacetime. It is a theoretically well-motivated black hole alternative and offers a potential observationally testable arena for probing strong-field gravity with horizon-scale images. We perform general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations and general relativistic radiative transfer (GRRT) calculations of accretion flows onto a Kerr-like wormhole. Adopting a Kerr black-bounce metric with a fixed throat parameter $\ell = 2.5\,\rm M$, we explore the effects of spin using both two- and three-dimensional simulations. The accretion flow is initialized as a magnetized geometrically thick torus near one mouth of the wormhole, while the opposite mouth is initially gas-free. We find that the spin parameter influences the dynamical properties on both sides of the wormhole through the frame-dragging effects. Based on the GRMHD results, we compute ray-traced images at $230\,\mathrm{GHz}$ using \texttt{RAPTOR}, and analyze the horizon-scale image structure through higher-order photon trajectories. Our GRRT calculations show that emissions originating from the immediate vicinity of the throat can dominate, in contrast to the case of a Kerr black hole. It provides the variable component of the signal and imprints a clear quasi-periodic modulation in the light curves. These properties would be useful to either confirm or rule out such exotic compact objects through horizon-scale observations.

AI.tldr: The paper simulates accretion flows onto a Kerr-like wormhole using GRMHD and GRRT, finding that throat emission dominates over black hole-like features and produces quasi-periodic modulations, offering observational tests to distinguish wormholes from black holes.
AI.motivation: Wormholes are theoretically motivated black hole alternatives that offer a testable arena for strong-field gravity; the goal is to identify observable signatures in horizon-scale images that could distinguish wormholes from black holes.
AI.method: GRMHD simulations (2D and 3D) of magnetized accretion onto a Kerr-like wormhole (Kerr black-bounce metric, throat parameter ℓ=2.5M) are performed, followed by GRRT calculations using RAPTOR at 230 GHz to compute ray-traced images and light curves.
AI.result: Spin influences dynamics on both wormhole sides via frame-dragging; emissions from the throat vicinity can dominate, unlike for Kerr black holes, and produce quasi-periodic modulations in light curves.
AI.conclusion: The distinct emission and variability signatures from wormhole throats can be used to confirm or rule out such exotic compact objects through horizon-scale observations.

title: Matter Clustering in Astrid: Reduced Baryonic Suppression from Realistic Black Hole Dynamics
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 1 table + Appendix (4 figures, 1 table); submitted to ApJL
summary: Baryonic feedback from active galactic nuclei (AGN) is often invoked as a major source of suppression in the matter power spectrum, with implications for precision cosmology and the $S_8$ tension. We present Astrid-DMO, the dark matter-only counterpart to the large-volume Astrid hydrodynamical simulation, and measure baryonic effects through $P_{\rm hydro}(k)/P_{\rm DMO}(k)$. We find no significant suppression at $z=0$ and mild suppression at $z=0.2$, weaker than in other state-of-the-art simulations. Using controlled small-volume runs, we identify a key driver of this discrepancy: the treatment of black hole (BH) dynamics. The widely used BH repositioning scheme artificially enhances BH mergers and boosts kinetic AGN feedback (e.g., by a factor of $2$ at $z=1.5$), leading to overly strong suppression. By contrast, a more physical dynamical friction model reduces feedback efficiency and weakens clustering suppression. Consequently, reconciling large-scale structure measurements with cosmic microwave background (CMB)-inferred $Λ$CDM cosmology with AGN feedback becomes more challenging. Although strengthening AGN feedback can increase suppression, in our model this induces tensions with the observed galaxy stellar mass and AGN luminosity functions. These results motivate considering either new non-baryonic physics that suppresses late-time matter clustering, or novel mechanisms that can efficiently eject gas from halos without compromising other galaxy properties.

AI.tldr: Using the Astrid-DMO simulation, this paper finds that AGN feedback causes weaker suppression of the matter power spectrum than other simulations, largely due to differences in black hole dynamics treatment—specifically, repositioning schemes artificially boost feedback, while a dynamical friction model yields more physical, weaker suppression.
AI.motivation: To understand the role of baryonic AGN feedback in suppressing the matter power spectrum, which has implications for precision cosmology and the S8 tension.
AI.method: Compare the hydrodynamical Astrid simulation with its dark matter-only counterpart (Astrid-DMO) to measure baryonic effects via P_hydro/P_DMO, and conduct controlled small-volume runs to isolate the impact of black hole dynamics treatments.
AI.result: No significant suppression at z=0, mild suppression at z=0.2, weaker than other simulations. BH repositioning artificially boosts mergers and kinetic feedback (e.g., factor of 2 at z=1.5), causing overly strong suppression; a dynamical friction model reduces feedback efficiency and weakens suppression.
AI.conclusion: Reconciling LSS measurements with CMB-inferred ΛCDM cosmology via AGN feedback becomes more challenging. Strengthening feedback to increase suppression conflicts with observed galaxy stellar mass and AGN luminosity functions. New non-baryonic physics or novel gas ejection mechanisms may be needed.

title: Theoretical Constraints on Neutron Star Superfluidity from Her X-1 Precession
comment: Submitted. Comments are very welcome
summary: Recent IXPE observations of Her X-1 reveal correlations between flux, polarization degree, and polarization angle across its 35-day superorbital cycle. These measurements have been interpreted as strong evidence that the 35-day period is driven by nearly free precession of the neutron star. We show that this interpretation carries far-reaching implications for the dynamics of the crustal superfluid. In particular, maintaining precession over the $\sim 50$-year observational baseline of Her X-1 would require that superfluid vortices remain unpinned for centuries and experience extremely weak mutual friction while traversing the heavy-ion lattice of the inner crust -- conditions that challenge conventional wisdom and standard models of glitch dynamics. Under the condition of weak pinning, nearly free precession of the crust may be sustained by a balance between the internal and external torques.

AI.tldr: IXPE observations of Her X-1 suggest its 35-day cycle is driven by neutron star free precession, requiring crustal superfluid vortices to remain unpinned for centuries with very weak mutual friction—challenging standard glitch models—potentially sustained by a balance of internal and external torques.
AI.motivation: To interpret recent IXPE observations of Her X-1 that correlate flux, polarization degree, and polarization angle over its 35-day superorbital cycle, and to explore the implications for neutron star crustal superfluid dynamics.
AI.method: Analysis of observational correlations (flux, polarization degree, polarization angle) from IXPE data across the 35-day cycle, combined with theoretical modeling of superfluid vortex pinning and mutual friction dynamics in the neutron star inner crust under the precession interpretation.
AI.result: Maintaining precession over ~50 years requires superfluid vortices to remain unpinned for centuries and experience extremely weak mutual friction while moving through the heavy-ion lattice of the inner crust, conditions that contradict conventional glitch models.
AI.conclusion: Nearly free precession of the crust may be sustained under weak pinning conditions by a balance between internal and external torques, but this demands unconventional superfluid properties that challenge standard theoretical frameworks.

title: A CNN--Transformer Denoiser for low-$S/N$ Galaxy Spectra: Stellar Population Recovery in Synthetic Tests
comment: 11 pages, 8 Figures, Published in AJ
summary: Stellar population measurements in integral field unit surveys are often limited by low signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) in low-surface-brightness spaxels. Using controlled synthetic experiments, we test whether deep-learning-based denoising can recover stellar population information without spatial binning. We introduce the Enhanced U-Net Transformer (EUT), a one-dimensional CNN-Transformer model trained on 90,000 synthetic spectra constructed from MILES simple stellar population models following Lee et al. (2023). Wavelength-dependent noise is injected on the fly to emulate SAMI-like data with S/N = 5-20, measured in a 4484.77-4573.12 Angstrom continuum window. On an independent test set of 10,000 spectra, EUT reduces the full-spectrum RMS residual by about 96.5 percent at S/N = 5 and about 94 percent at S/N = 20, with recovery rates of at least 99.8 percent. In fixed windows around Ca II H, Hdelta, Hbeta, Fe I 4383, Mg b, and Na D, residuals decrease by more than about 88 percent while preserving line-profile structure. In downstream pPXF fitting, the RMS scatter in recovered mass-weighted age decreases from about 0.41 to 0.25 dex at S/N = 5 and from about 0.32 to 0.22 dex at S/N = 10. For mass-weighted metallicity, [M/H], the scatter decreases from about 0.45 to 0.36 dex and from about 0.32 to 0.28 dex, respectively. At S/N = 20, denoised and noisy inputs give consistent results within the synthetic-test uncertainties. These experiments suggest that hybrid CNN-Transformer denoisers can improve low-S/N spectra for stellar population studies, although validation with observed spectra is still required.

AI.tldr: The Enhanced U-Net Transformer (EUT), a 1D CNN-Transformer denoising model, significantly reduces noise in low-S/N synthetic IFU spectra (S/N=5-20), recovering stellar population parameters (age, metallicity) more accurately than noisy inputs without spatial binning.
AI.motivation: Stellar population measurements in IFU surveys are limited by low S/N in low-surface-brightness spaxels; spatial binning is commonly used but sacrifices resolution. Deep-learning-based denoising offers a potential alternative to recover information without binning.
AI.method: Introduces the Enhanced U-Net Transformer (EUT), a 1D CNN-Transformer model trained on 90,000 synthetic MILES SSP spectra with on-the-fly wavelength-dependent noise injection to emulate SAMI-like data at S/N=5-20. Tested on 10,000 independent spectra, evaluated via RMS residuals, line-profile preservation, and downstream pPXF fitting for age and metallicity recovery.
AI.result: EUT reduces full-spectrum RMS residual by ~96.5% at S/N=5 and ~94% at S/N=20, with >99.8% recovery rates. Line-profile residuals around key absorption features decrease by >88%. In pPXF fitting, mass-weighted age RMS scatter decreases from 0.41→0.25 dex (S/N=5) and 0.32→0.22 dex (S/N=10); metallicity scatter decreases from 0.45→0.36 dex and 0.32→0.28 dex respectively. At S/N=20, denoised and noisy results are consistent.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid CNN-Transformer denoisers (EUT) can improve low-S/N spectra for stellar population studies, reducing RMS residuals by ~94-96.5% and improving downstream age/metallicity estimates, though validation with observed spectra is still required.

title: Confirmation of Binary Clustering in Gamma-Ray Bursts through an Integrated $p$-value from Multiple Nonparametric Tests of Hypotheses
summary: The paper applies a new, nonparametric, interpoint distance-based measure to confirm the inherent groups prevailing in the brightest source of light in the universe: gamma-ray bursts. Our effective metric, in association with clustering methods like Gaussian-mixture model-based and $K$-means algorithms, resolves the conflict regarding the possibility about existence of more than binary clusters in the gamma-ray burst population. Here we carry out multiple nonparametric statistical tests of hypotheses, as many as the number of bursts available from the `BATSE' catalog. An integrated $p$-value achieved from the aforesaid dependent tests solves our concern confirming two groups of short and long bursts.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a nonparametric interpoint distance-based measure with clustering algorithms (Gaussian-mixture and K-means) to confirm that gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) form two distinct groups (short and long), resolving the debate about whether more than two clusters exist in the GRB population. The analysis is supported by multiple nonparametric statistical tests on BATSE catalog data with an integrated p-value.
AI.motivation: To resolve the ongoing debate about whether gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) form more than two distinct groups, by applying a new nonparametric interpoint distance-based measure to confirm the inherent groupings in GRB populations.
AI.method: A nonparametric interpoint distance-based measure combined with Gaussian-mixture model-based and K-means clustering algorithms, along with multiple nonparametric statistical hypothesis tests using BATSE catalog data and an integrated p-value from dependent tests.
AI.result: The integrated p-value from multiple nonparametric tests confirms two distinct groups of short and long gamma-ray bursts, resolving the conflict about the existence of more than binary clusters.
AI.conclusion: The proposed nonparametric metric successfully confirms a binary classification (short vs. long) of gamma-ray bursts, settling the controversy regarding the number of inherent groups in the GRB population.

title: Exact solutions, trajectories and radiation patterns in the classical relativistic Störmer problem
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures
summary: We investigate the relativistic generalization of the classical Störmer problem, which describes the motion of charged particles in a purely magnetic dipole field. By incorporating special relativistic effects, the particle dynamics is governed by a strongly nonlinear system of second-order differential equations derived from the Lorentz force law. We present a rigorous and fully covariant derivation of the relativistic equations of motion, together with the associated conservation laws. An exact solution for planar motions is obtained in parametric form, providing analytical insight into the structure of the trajectories. In addition, we perform a detailed numerical analysis of the particle dynamics across both nonrelativistic and relativistic regimes, exploring a range of initial conditions and highlighting the impact of relativistic corrections. The electromagnetic radiation emitted by the accelerated charges is also examined. We compute the time dependence of the total radiated power and determine the corresponding frequency spectrum. Our results provide a comprehensive characterization of magnetic dipole--type radiation associated with Störmer-like motion. In particular, the power spectral density consistently exhibits distinct peaks, indicating the presence of preferred frequency bands in the emitted radiation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a relativistic generalization of the classical Störmer problem for charged particles in a magnetic dipole field. The authors derive covariant equations of motion from the Lorentz force law, find an exact parametric solution for planar motions, perform numerical analysis across nonrelativistic and relativistic regimes, and compute the radiated power and frequency spectrum, revealing distinct peaks in the power spectral density indicative of preferred frequency bands.
AI.motivation: To extend the classical Störmer problem (charged particle motion in a magnetic dipole field) into the relativistic regime, providing a rigorous theoretical framework and analytical insights that account for special relativistic effects and the associated electromagnetic radiation.
AI.method: The authors derive relativistic equations of motion from the Lorentz force law in a fully covariant manner, obtain an exact parametric solution for planar motion, perform numerical simulations across relativistic and nonrelativistic regimes, and compute the total radiated power and frequency spectrum of the emitted electromagnetic radiation.
AI.result: An exact parametric solution for planar motions is obtained. Numerical analysis reveals the impact of relativistic corrections on trajectory dynamics. The computed power spectral density consistently exhibits distinct peaks, indicating preferred frequency bands in the emitted magnetic dipole-type radiation.
AI.conclusion: The relativistic generalization of the Störmer problem yields a comprehensive characterization of charged particle dynamics and associated radiation, with the distinct spectral peaks suggesting structured frequency signatures in Störmer-like magnetic dipole radiation.

title: AGILE detection of transient γ-ray emission from the region of the supergiant fast X-ray transient source IGR J17354-3255
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A
summary:
Context. On April 14, 2009, the AGILE satellite detected a γ-ray flare from an unknown transient source. Subsequent X-ray follow-up observations with Swift and INTEGRAL identified the supergiant fast X-ray transient (SFXT) IGR J17354-3255 as the best candidate counterpart, based on positional coincidence and a similar temporal behaviour. Aside from this hint, no SFXT has been firmly detected at high energies to date. Overall, SFXTs comprise a subclass of high-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs) that host a massive OB supergiant star as a companion donor. They tend to display the most extreme X-ray variability among HMXBs. These systems might be able to emit photons at MeV-TeV energies in the form of fast flares lasting from hours to a few days, with a low-duty cycle.
  Aims. In this work, we analyse archival AGILE data to search for γ-ray flares consistent with IGR J17354-3255 and evaluate their possible physical origin.
  Methods. We identified a transient source, AGL J1736-3250, which emitted 19 γ-ray flares and was seen to be positionally consistent with IGR J17354-3255. Most flares, detected on a 1 d timescale, concentrate most of their emission on two, four, and six hour timescales, resembling those observed in the X-ray band from IGR J17354-3255.
  Results. An orbital phase analysis revealed that approximately half of the γ-ray activity occurs around the apastron passage of the compact object hosted in the binary system. We also incorporated archival Swift and INTEGRAL observations to provide phase-folded light curves at lower energies. Our collected results strongly support a physical association between IGR J17354-3255 and AGL J1736-3250, offering evidence that SFXTs could constitute a new class of Galactic high-energy transient emitters.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the detection of 19 γ-ray flares from AGL J1736-3250, positionally consistent with the SFXT IGR J17354-3255. Orbital phase analysis shows about half of the γ-ray activity occurs near apastron, strongly supporting a physical association and suggesting SFXTs may be a new class of Galactic high-energy transient emitters.
AI.motivation: To analyze archival AGILE data for γ-ray flares consistent with IGR J17354-3255 and evaluate their physical origin, given that SFXTs are a subclass of HMXBs with extreme X-ray variability and potential for MeV-TeV emission.
AI.method: Archival AGILE data analysis to search for γ-ray flares; cross-correlation with positional data from IGR J17354-3255; temporal analysis on 1-day, 2-hour, 4-hour, and 6-hour timescales; orbital phase analysis; incorporation of Swift and INTEGRAL observations to produce phase-folded lower-energy light curves.
AI.result: Identified 19 γ-ray flares from AGL J1736-3250 consistent with IGR J17354-3255. Most flares concentrate emission on 2–6 hour timescales. ~50% of γ-ray activity occurs near apastron. Phase-folded light curves from Swift/INTEGRAL support the association.
AI.conclusion: Strong evidence supports a physical association between IGR J17354-3255 and AGL J1736-3250, indicating that SFXTs may constitute a new class of Galactic high-energy (γ-ray) transient emitters.

title: A spectroscopic map of the Galactic centre: Integrated light and dynamical modelling
comment: 11 pages (+ 5 pages Appendix), 9 (+ 5) figures, accepted A&A
summary: The centre of the Milky Way is occupied by a nuclear star cluster, which contains the supermassive black hole Sgr A*. The cluster is embedded in the larger surrounding nuclear stellar disc. These three components dominate the mass budget of the Galactic centre at different radial scales. The mass distribution of the Galactic centre has been studied extensively using observations of individual bright stars and various dynamical modelling approaches. The situation differs for external galaxies, where observations are often limited to the integrated line-of-sight kinematics. For such systems, triaxial orbit-based dynamical modelling has become a standard method to derive mass distributions and stellar orbit distributions. We aim to apply and test this method on the Galactic centre. We extract stellar line-of-sight kinematic maps of the inner ~3 pc x 66 pc region of the Galactic centre. We use the DYNAMITE code, which calculates an orbit library in a given gravitational potential and computes model kinematic maps. These maps are then compared to the observed kinematic maps, and the gravitational potential and orbit distribution of the Galactic centre are constrained. We recover the correct mass of Sgr A*, and our stellar mass distributions are in agreement with the literature, albeit with larger uncertainties. The stellar structures are at most mildly triaxial and close to oblate. The stellar orbit distribution in the inner region is dominated by dynamically warm and hot orbits. At larger scales, dynamically cold, that is, highly rotating orbits, have the largest weights. The dominance of hot and warm orbits is a consequence of short dynamical timescales in the inner Galactic centre, causing dynamical heating. The presence of cold orbits at large radii may be explained by the longer heating timescales in this region, and if the stars in the outer nuclear stellar disc are younger.[abridged]

AI.tldr: The paper applies triaxial orbit-based dynamical modeling (DYNAMITE) to the Milky Way's Galactic centre, using stellar line-of-sight kinematic maps of the inner ~3 pc x 66 pc region to constrain the mass distribution and orbital structure. It recovers the correct mass of Sgr A*, finds stellar structures are mildly triaxial/close to oblate, and reveals a transition from hot/warm orbits in the inner region to cold (rotating) orbits at larger radii, attributed to dynamical heating timescales.
AI.motivation: To apply and test triaxial orbit-based dynamical modelling—a standard method for external galaxies—on the Galactic centre, where direct stellar observations are available, in order to validate the method and derive the mass distribution and stellar orbit distribution.
AI.method: Extract stellar line-of-sight kinematic maps of the inner ~3 pc x 66 pc region; use the DYNAMITE code to compute an orbit library in a given gravitational potential, generate model kinematic maps, and compare them to observed maps to constrain the gravitational potential and orbit distribution.
AI.result: Recovered the correct mass of Sgr A*; stellar mass distributions agree with literature (with larger uncertainties); stellar structures are mildly triaxial and close to oblate; inner region dominated by dynamically warm/hot orbits; outer region dominated by dynamically cold (highly rotating) orbits.
AI.conclusion: The dominance of hot/warm orbits in the inner region results from short dynamical timescales causing dynamical heating; cold orbits at large radii are explained by longer heating timescales and possibly younger stellar populations in the outer nuclear stellar disc.

title: Bayesian parameter estimation for the Core-bounce phase of Rapidly Rotating Core-Collapse Supernovae in real interferometric data
comment: 17 pages, 13 figures
summary: We present a novel methodology to estimate the ratio of kinetic to gravitational potential energy in core-collapse supernova progenitors and to assess the equation of state (EOS) using gravitational-wave signals from the core-bounce phase of rapidly rotating stars in real interferometric data. We extend a previous phenomenological model by introducing an additional parameter that captures the signal timescale. The agreement between our template and numerical waveform databases is evaluated through fitting factors and Bayesian model comparison, also assessing consistency across datasets. The improved model increases the median fitting factor from 88.88% to 90.83%. Parameter estimation is performed via Markov Chain Monte Carlo using real O3aL1 noise. For 452 simulated signals, the rotational parameter $β$ is recovered with a median relative error of 11.93% (95th percentile: 38.41%) and an uncertainty of $σ_β= 1.083 \times 10^{-3}$ at 10 kpc, improving over previous matched-filtering results. We further analyze the impact of prior choices and noise properties, finding that real interferometric noise introduces biases up to 11.9%, while optimized priors can reduce them to 0.6%.

AI.tldr: A novel methodology estimates the kinetic-to-potential energy ratio (β) in core-collapse supernova progenitors and assesses the equation of state using gravitational-wave signals from core-bounce in rapidly rotating stars. An improved phenomenological template (adding a timescale parameter) raises the median fitting factor from 88.88% to 90.83%. Using MCMC on real O3aL1 noise, β is recovered with median relative error 11.93% at 10 kpc; real noise introduces biases up to 11.9%, reduced to 0.6% with optimized priors.
AI.motivation: To enable inference of progenitor properties (specifically the rotational parameter β) and the nuclear equation of state from gravitational-wave signals of rapidly rotating core-collapse supernovae, which current template-based methods handle with limited accuracy and without accounting for real detector noise characteristics.
AI.method: Extended a phenomenological signal model by adding a timescale parameter; evaluated template fidelity via fitting factors and Bayesian model comparison against numerical waveform databases; performed parameter estimation with Markov Chain Monte Carlo using real O3aL1 LIGO noise; analyzed 452 simulated signals under varied priors and noise conditions.
AI.result: Median fitting factor increased from 88.88% to 90.83%; β recovery achieved 11.93% median relative error (95th percentile: 38.41%) and uncertainty σ_β = 1.083×10⁻³ at 10 kpc; real noise introduces biases up to 11.9%, reducible to 0.6% with optimized priors.
AI.conclusion: The improved template enables more accurate inference of rotational energy ratios and EOS constraints from gravitational-wave observations of core-collapse supernovae, and highlights the critical importance of prior optimization and realistic noise modeling for reliable parameter estimation in real detector data.

title: The MeerKAT Massive Distant Clusters Survey: a search for diffuse radio emission in 30 massive SZ-selected clusters at $z > 1$
comment: 23 pages, 15 figures, 4 tables. Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We present the results of a search for diffuse radio emission in a uniformly selected sample of 30 of the most massive Sunyaev-Zel'dovich selected galaxy clusters at $z > 1$, providing the first statistical constraints on the evolution of cluster-scale diffuse emission beyond this redshift. We also analyse the scaling relations between radio power ($P_{1.4\,\mathrm{GHz}}$) and cluster mass ($M_{\rm 500c}$) in this high-redshift sample. It is well established that radio halos are primarily found in the most massive clusters, where turbulent energy from major mergers can re-accelerate relativistic electrons and amplify magnetic fields on megaparsec scales. Deep MeerKAT 1.28 GHz observations reveal diffuse radio halos in eight clusters (27$\%$), while the remaining 21 (70$\%$) show no emission; one additional cluster (3$\%$) was excluded from the radio analysis due to poor data quality. The halo detection rate in this high-redshift sample is lower than at intermediate redshift, but remains higher than the $\lesssim 10\%$ occurrence generally predicted by theoretical models at $z \gtrsim 1$. The detected radio halos scatter around the best-fitting $P_{1.4\,\mathrm{GHz}}$-$M_{\rm 500c}^{\rm {Unc}}$ relation derived for the MMDCS sample, whereas non-detections populate the lower envelope of the radio power-mass plane, similar to trends seen at lower redshift. No cluster-scale radio relics or mini-halos are identified. Our findings highlight MeerKAT's ability to probe non-thermal processes in the most distant clusters and the need for deeper, lower-frequency surveys to uncover faint diffuse emission and test the persistence of the $P_{1.4\,\mathrm{GHz}}$-$M_{\rm 500}$ relation across cosmic time.

AI.tldr: A search for diffuse radio emission in 30 massive galaxy clusters at z>1 using MeerKAT finds 8 radio halos (27% detection rate), lower than at intermediate redshift but higher than theoretical predictions of <10%. Detected halos follow the P-M relation, while non-detections occupy the lower envelope. No relics or mini-halos found.
AI.motivation: To provide the first statistical constraints on the evolution of cluster-scale diffuse radio emission in galaxy clusters at z>1, and to test whether the radio power-cluster mass scaling relation persists at high redshift.
AI.method: Uniformly selected sample of 30 most massive Sunyaev-Zel'dovich selected galaxy clusters at z>1 observed with deep MeerKAT 1.28 GHz observations. Radio halos identified, detection rates computed, and P_{1.4 GHz}-M_{500c} scaling relations analyzed.
AI.result: 8 clusters (27%) show diffuse radio halos, 21 (70%) show no emission, 1 excluded. Detection rate lower than at intermediate redshift but higher than theoretical predictions of <10% at z>1. Detected halos scatter around the P-M relation; non-detections lie on the lower envelope. No radio relics or mini-halos found.
AI.conclusion: MeerKAT demonstrates capability to probe non-thermal processes in distant clusters. Deeper, lower-frequency surveys are needed to uncover faint emission and test the persistence of the P-M relation across cosmic time.

title: Sensitivity of the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory to Gamma-Ray Signals in Dwarf Irregular Galaxies
comment: 47 pages, 30 figures
summary: Dwarf irregular galaxies (dIrrs) are rotationally supported galaxies with a low star formation rate. Thus, their gamma-ray astrophysical emission is expected to be low, making them interesting targets for WIMP dark matter (DM) indirect searches. In this work, we build upon previous work on these objects in this DM context, and identify the best four dIrrs to be observed by the forthcoming Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO). Since dIrrs have not been detected in gamma rays yet, we first explore the prospects for detecting their astrophysical emission with the CTAO. Secondly, we compute the CTAO sensitivity prospects to a DM annihilating signal from these objects, accounting for the presence of DM substructures in them. We do so for both cuspy and cored DM density profiles, as the cusp-core debate remains particularly open for dIrrs. Our best combined limits show the potential to exclude DM annihilation cross-section values around $2\times 10^{-24} \ \mathrm{cm^{3}}\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ for 100 GeV WIMP masses annihilating in the $τ^+τ^-$ channel. These prospective results are competitive with and complementary to benchmark targets such as galaxy clusters. We also analyze the case of the velocity-dependent annihilation cross-section (Sommerfeld enhancement), obtaining projected DM constraints that exceed those expected for dwarf spheroidal galaxies, thanks to the contribution of subhalos to the signal. We conclude that dIrrs are compelling targets for the CTAO, not only for DM indirect searches but also as possible astrophysical sources.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates dwarf irregular galaxies (dIrrs) as targets for the CTAO, finding competitive sensitivity for WIMP dark matter indirect detection (down to ~2×10⁻²⁴ cm³ s⁻¹ for 100 GeV in the τ⁺τ⁻ channel) and showing that subhalo contributions enhance constraints, especially for velocity-dependent annihilation (Sommerfeld enhancement), outperforming dwarf spheroidal galaxies.
AI.motivation: Dwarf irregular galaxies have low star formation rates and thus low expected gamma-ray astrophysical emission, making them clean targets for WIMP dark matter indirect searches. The paper aims to identify the best dIrrs for CTAO observations and assess their detectability.
AI.method: The authors select the four best dIrrs for CTAO, compute prospective astrophysical gamma-ray detectability, and derive CTAO sensitivity for dark matter annihilation signals. They account for DM substructures and consider both cuspy and cored DM density profiles, as well as velocity-dependent (Sommerfeld-enhanced) annihilation cross-sections.
AI.result: Best combined limits can exclude DM annihilation cross-sections of ~2×10⁻²⁴ cm³ s⁻¹ for 100 GeV WIMPs in the τ⁺τ⁻ channel. These results are competitive with galaxy cluster benchmarks. For Sommerfeld enhancement, projected constraints exceed those for dwarf spheroidal galaxies due to subhalo signal contributions.
AI.conclusion: Dwarf irregular galaxies are compelling targets for the CTAO, both for dark matter indirect searches and as potential astrophysical gamma-ray sources.

title: Compact, AGN-hosting Dwarf Galaxies with "Little Red Dots"-like SEDs in the Local Universe
comment: 15 pages, 11 figures. Revised version submitted to ApJ. Comments welcome
summary: Local active galactic nuclei (AGNs) in dwarf galaxies are often considered as analogs for the earliest supermassive black holes, although their connections require more comprehensive examinations. Motivated by finding the local analogs of "Little Red Dots" (LRDs), the compact, red galaxies discovered by JWST at z > 5 characterized by "V-shaped" SEDs, we compile a sample of local AGN-hosting dwarf galaxies (ADGs) with comparable luminosities to statistically evaluate this connection. By applying K-means clustering to SED shapes and morphological sizes, we classified four groups which trace a sequence in physical properties, including metallicity, star formation rate, and dust emission, mainly driven by their distinct UV-optical slopes. Within these groups, we find that about half of the ADGs exhibit "V-shaped" SEDs and relatively compact morphologies. However, a direct comparison reveals fundamental physical differences: local "V-shaped", compact ADGs appear significantly more evolved than high-z LRDs, characterized by systematically larger effective radii and distinct ionization states. Our results suggest that local compact ADGs likely follow a different formation pathway from LRDs, highlighting the complexity of black hole-galaxy co-evolution across cosmic time.

AI.tldr: Local AGN-hosting dwarf galaxies (ADGs) classified via K-means clustering include some with "V-shaped" SEDs and compact morphologies akin to high-z LRDs, but they are more evolved (larger radii, distinct ionization), suggesting different formation pathways.
AI.motivation: To find local analogs of JWST-discovered "Little Red Dots" (LRDs) at z > 5, using local AGN-hosting dwarf galaxies as possible counterparts for studying early supermassive black hole connections.
AI.method: Compiled a sample of local AGN-hosting dwarf galaxies (ADGs) with comparable luminosities to LRDs; applied K-means clustering based on SED shapes and morphological sizes to classify groups.
AI.result: Four groups classified, tracing a sequence in metallicity, SFR, and dust emission driven by UV-optical slopes; ~half of ADGs show "V-shaped" SEDs and compact morphologies, but they are systematically more evolved (larger effective radii, distinct ionization states) than high-z LRDs.
AI.conclusion: Local compact ADGs likely follow a different formation pathway from high-z LRDs, highlighting the complexity of black-hole galaxy co-evolution across cosmic time.

title: Parameter Estimation Horizon of Core-Collapse Supernovae with Current and Next-Generation Gravitational-Wave Detectors
comment: Submitted to PRD. Comments are welcome
summary: Core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) are powerful sources of gravitational waves (GWs). These signals propagate essentially unobstructed, providing a unique probe of the supernova central engine. In this work, we investigate parameter estimation from the bounce and early ring-down GW signal of rotating CCSNe using machine learning. We infer the peak frequency and peak amplitude of the signal as well as the rotation of the core. We extend previous studies in several directions. We consider a range of progenitor models and nuclear equations of state, and we assess the impact of key physical uncertainties, including bounce-time uncertainty and source inclination. We incorporate both current detector noise and the projected sensitivities of next-generation observatories. We find that uncertainty in the bounce time does not significantly affect parameter estimation when the analysis is performed in the Fourier domain. In contrast, orientations when the rotation axis is near the line of sight substantially degrade performance. For optimal orientations, next-generation detectors can constrain rotation out to distances exceeding 100 kpc.

AI.tldr: This study uses machine learning to estimate parameters (peak frequency, amplitude, core rotation) from the bounce and early ring-down GW signal of rotating CCSNe, finding that bounce-time uncertainty has minimal impact while source inclination significantly affects performance, with next-generation detectors capable of constraining rotation beyond 100 kpc under optimal orientations.
AI.motivation: CCSNe produce gravitational waves that propagate unobstructed and offer a unique probe of the supernova central engine. The goal is to infer key physical parameters from these GW signals using machine learning, extending previous work by considering diverse progenitors, equations of state, and physical uncertainties.
AI.method: Machine learning-based parameter estimation applied to the bounce and early ring-down GW signal of rotating CCSNe. The analysis incorporates multiple progenitor models, nuclear equations of state, bounce-time uncertainty, source inclination, and both current and next-generation detector noise models.
AI.result: Bounce-time uncertainty does not significantly affect parameter estimation in the Fourier domain. Orientations with the rotation axis near the line of sight substantially degrade performance. Under optimal orientations, next-generation detectors can constrain rotation out to distances exceeding 100 kpc.
AI.conclusion: Machine learning enables robust parameter estimation from CCSN GW signals, with source inclination being the dominant limiting factor. Next-generation observatories will dramatically extend the reach for rotation constraints.

title: The one and the only: the pulsar - white dwarf system in NGC 6749
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, two tables. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: PSR J1905+0154A is a binary millisecond pulsar located in the globular cluster (GC) NGC 6749. It was discovered in 2004 in a search for pulsars in GCs carried out with the Arecibo 305-m radio telescope. The pulsar has a spin period of 3.2 ms, an orbital period of 0.81 days, and is in a low-eccentricity orbit with a low-mass WD companion. Combining early Arecibo and latter Five Hundred meter Aperture Spherical Telescope (FAST) data, we were able to derive a phase-coherent timing solution for this pulsar, which now spans 20 years. This includes a precise measurement of the astrometric, spin and orbital parameters of the system. The small range of predicted accelerations expected from the gravitational field of this GC allows an estimate of the intrinsic spin-down: the inferred magnetic field at the surface (2.2 - 2.4 * 10^8 G) and characteristic age (2.8 - 3.5 Gyr) are typical of what one finds among MSPs in the Galactic field. The position of this pulsar coincides with the position of one of the very few candidate white dwarfs (WDs) in the whole HST dataset on this GC. The position of the companion in the colour-magnitude diagram is consistent with a Helium WD with a mass of 0.17 - 0.19 M_sun, a cooling age of 0.4 - 0.7 Gyr, and a surface temperature of 11,600 - 14,800 K. A comparison with the characteristic age of the pulsar indicates that at the start of the WD cooling the latter had a spin period of ~2.7 ms. The velocity of the system relative to the GC, which is 4.5-sigma significant and an order of magnitude larger than the escape velocity, raises the possibility that, despite its location close to the centre of the GC, the pulsar might not be associated with it. Finally, our effort to confirm a second pulsar candidate in this GC did not yield a positive confirmation, nor the discovery of any additional pulsar in this GC.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a 20-year phase-coherent timing solution for PSR J1905+0154A, a 3.2-ms binary pulsar in GC NGC 6749, deriving its intrinsic spin-down, magnetic field, and characteristic age, identifying its WD companion via HST data, and questioning the pulsar's association with the cluster due to an anomalously high relative velocity.
AI.motivation: To derive a precise, long-baseline timing solution for PSR J1905+0154A to measure its astrometric, spin, and orbital parameters, characterize its WD companion, and investigate the pulsar's association with the globular cluster NGC 6749.
AI.method: Combined early Arecibo 305-m and latter FAST radio telescope data spanning 20 years to obtain a phase-coherent timing solution; compared pulsar position with HST photometry to identify and characterize the WD companion via color-magnitude diagram fitting; used predicted cluster acceleration field to estimate intrinsic spin-down parameters.
AI.result: Obtained precise timing solution; derived surface magnetic field 2.2–2.4×10⁸ G and characteristic age 2.8–3.5 Gyr; identified companion as a He WD of mass 0.17–0.19 M☉ with cooling age 0.4–0.7 Gyr and temperature 11,600–14,800 K; found pulsar's relative velocity to GC is 4.5σ significant and exceeds escape velocity by ~10×, questioning cluster association; did not confirm a second pulsar candidate.
AI.conclusion: PSR J1905+0154A is a typical MSP in terms of magnetic field and age; the WD companion properties are consistent with a low-mass He WD; the anomalously high relative velocity suggests the pulsar may be a foreground or background object not bound to NGC 6749 despite its central location.

title: Statistical evidence for massive black hole recoils in active galactic nuclei
comment: 11 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables, submitted to MNRAS
summary: We search for a population-level signature of gravitational-wave recoiling supermassive black holes: a positive correlation between dust obscuration and the magnitude of the line-of-sight velocity offset of broad emission lines relative to the host. Using the SDSS DR16 quasar catalogue, we estimate the velocity offset, $Δv$, as the difference between the broad H$β$ redshift and a noise-weighted redshift from narrow lines ([O III] 5007, [O II] 3728, and Ca II 3934). We adopt the redshift-relative colour excess $Δ(g-i)$ as a proxy for dust column density. Analysing $\sim10^{5}$ quasars that meet basic spectral quality requirements, we find a modest but highly significant positive correlation between $|Δv|$ and $Δ(g-i)$ (Spearman $r\simeq0.12$ and Pearson $r\simeq0.13$, with $p\ll10^{-10}$ in both cases). The fraction of highly obscured quasars increases with $|Δv|$, indicating that the correlation is driven by a dust-reddened subpopulation. The result is robust to the choice of minimum $|Δv|$ threshold and to the line redshift estimator (peak vs. centroid). As expected, the correlation is largely absent when velocity offsets are computed between narrow emission lines. We find systematic differences between redshifted and blueshifted subsamples, which may point to residual velocity biases or additional physical effects (e.g. winds, inflows, orientation-dependent obscuration, or asymmetric broad-line regions). Recoiling massive black holes provide a natural explanation for the observed correlation, but alternative scenarios should be explored. If confirmed, this would enable population-level constraints on massive black hole merger rates, recoil dynamics, and active galactic nuclei disc properties.

AI.tldr: Using ~10^5 SDSS DR16 quasars, the paper finds a modest but highly significant positive correlation between broad-line velocity offset |Δv| and dust reddening Δ(g-i), consistent with expectations for recoiling supermassive black holes, though alternative explanations are not ruled out.
AI.motivation: To search for a population-level signature of gravitational-wave recoiling supermassive black holes by testing for a positive correlation between dust obscuration and line-of-sight velocity offsets of broad emission lines relative to the host galaxy.
AI.method: Used SDSS DR16 quasar catalogue (~10^5 objects); estimated velocity offset Δv as difference between broad Hβ redshift and noise-weighted narrow-line redshift ([O III], [O II], Ca II); adopted redshift-relative colour excess Δ(g-i) as proxy for dust column density; performed Spearman and Pearson correlation analyses.
AI.result: Modest but highly significant positive correlation between |Δv| and Δ(g-i) (Spearman r~0.12, Pearson r~0.13, p≪10^-10); correlation driven by dust-reddened subpopulation; robust to |Δv| threshold and redshift estimator choice; largely absent when using narrow-line velocity offsets; systematic differences between redshifted and blueshifted subsamples.
AI.conclusion: Recoiling massive black holes provide a natural explanation for the observed correlation, but alternative scenarios (winds, inflows, orientation-dependent obscuration, asymmetric BLRs) should be explored. If confirmed, this enables population-level constraints on MBH merger rates, recoil dynamics, and AGN disc properties.

title: Connecting the long-term variability behaviour of active galactic nuclei to their central engines
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. 14 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables
summary: Analysing the long-term radio variability of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) is essential to understanding the physics of relativistic jets launched by supermassive black holes. We aim to connect the characteristic timescales obtained from a prior power spectral density (PSD) analysis to the decomposed timescales of the light curves. In addition, we probe for potential associations between the timescales and the physical characteristics of the relativistic jet as well as the central engine. We decomposed the long-term radio light curves of 54 sources observed at the Aalto University Metsähovi Radio Observatory into individual flares to understand which timescale of variability is related to the low-frequency bend in the PSD. In addition, we used the obtained rise times of the brightest flares to look for associations between the emission-region size in the jet and different central engine parameters. We found that the inverse of the PSD bend frequency of radio light curves best corresponds to the mean duration of the brightest flares. For some sources, the mean flare separation had a similar timescale. Using the flare durations and separations as proxies for the PSD timescale, we found a positive correlation with black hole mass divided by the normalised mass accretion rate. This suggests that the variability timescales obtained from the PSDs of radio light curves are associated with the central engine. Furthermore, when comparing the obtained rise times of the brightest flares to the jet and central engine parameters, we found weak tentative correlations, but they may be driven by a common dependency on redshift.

AI.tldr: The study analyzes long-term radio variability of 54 AGNs using Metsähovi Radio Observatory data, finding that the inverse of PSD bend frequency corresponds to mean flare duration, and that variability timescales correlate with black hole mass and accretion rate, suggesting a connection to the central engine.
AI.motivation: To connect characteristic timescales from PSD analysis to decomposed light curve timescales, and to probe associations between these timescales and the physical properties of relativistic jets and the central engine in AGNs.
AI.method: Decomposed long-term radio light curves of 54 AGNs observed at Metsähovi Radio Observatory into individual flares; compared PSD bend frequencies with flare durations and separations; correlated flare rise times with jet and central engine parameters.
AI.result: The inverse PSD bend frequency corresponds best to the mean duration of the brightest flares; positive correlation found between PSD timescales and black hole mass divided by normalized mass accretion rate; weak tentative correlations between rise times and jet/central engine parameters, potentially driven by redshift dependence.
AI.conclusion: Radio variability timescales from PSD analysis are associated with the central engine properties (black hole mass and accretion rate), suggesting that long-term radio variability in AGNs is fundamentally linked to the supermassive black hole rather than solely jet physics.

title: Contribution of interstellar objects to local dark matter density
summary: The recent discovery of three interstellar comets in the solar system indicates the presence of so-far unaccounted baryonic matter in the Galaxy as a population of inter-stellar objects (ISO). The contribution of ISOs to the overall mass budget of the Galaxy affects the estimates on mass of the non-baryonic dark matter halo. We are attempting to estimate the mass density of non-baryonic Dark Matter after including a Galactic ISO contribution to the Galactic rotation curve. The object 3I/ATLAS is a surprisingly massive object with estimates of the nuclear radius reaching up to few kilo-metres. The observed incidence rate of interstellar objects (ISO) passing through the inner solar system in combination with estimates on the mass density and size provides an estimate of the local mass density if ISOs in the interstellar medium. The resulting estimate carries large uncertainties which are the consequence of the difficulties to constrain or measure the nuclear radius. The large kinematic age of 3I/ATLAS motivates a model where ISO objects are distributed in a thick (0.8~kpc) disk with a large radial scale length of $\approx 7$~kpc estimated from a fit to rotational velocity measurements from GAIA DR3 data. We find that the ISO contribution to the baryonic mass budget could reach a total mass of $5\times 10^{10}~M_\odot$ which leads to a reduction of the local Dark Matter halo density to $0.24$~GeV/cm$^3$. title: Little red dots as obscured little blue dots: relative abundances, luminosities, and black-hole masses
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, submitted
summary: We test whether ``little red dots'' (LRDs) are the dust-reddened, high-inclination counterparts of bluer compact broad-line active galactic nuclei, here referred to as ``little blue dots'' (LBDs), by modeling their relative number densities and luminosities. Using the observed UV luminosity function (LF) of broad-line active galactic nuclei (BLAGNs) at z>4 as the parent distribution, we forward-model the effects of accretion rate, anisotropic emission, orientation, and dust obscuration within our super-Eddington unification framework. We show that a model with a geometrically thick accretion flow, an equatorially concentrated broad-line region, and a dusty circumnuclear cloud population reproduces the LRD LF over the luminosity range currently constrained by JWST. The predicted LRD/BLAGN fraction is strongly luminosity dependent, rising from 3% at M_1500=-21 to a peak value of 20% near M_1500=-19. The model also predicts a larger apparent LRD fraction at rest-frame optical wavelengths, reaching 26% at M_4500=-20 mag and 35% at M_6500=-21. The best-fitting solutions imply a characteristic per-cloud extinction <A_V>=2.8^{+0.0}_{-0.4} mag and a mean dust covering factor <C_dust>= 0.23^{+0.27}_{-0.00} at 68% confidence, with the asymmetric uncertainties reflecting the degeneracy between cloud extinction and covering factor. These results may support an orientation-based unification of little dots and identify the LRD LF as a key demographic test of rapid accretion onto infant black holes at cosmic dawn. Within this same framework, UV-selected LRDs are predicted to host systematically more massive black holes than unobscured LBDs, not because they represent a distinct parent population, but because dust attenuation preferentially removes lower-mass obscured systems from the observed UV sample.

title: Near-infrared diagnostic diagrams of the gas ionization sources in nearby galaxies: a JWST NIRSpec view
comment: Accepted for publication
summary: Buried active galactic nuclei and obscured young stellar clusters pose significant challenges to traditional optical diagnostic diagrams. Therefore, developing new tools to trace the excitation sources across the spectrum is a necessary effort for the advancement of the field. Our goal is to explore the full spectral range of the JWST-NIRSpec data, searching for alternative diagnostic diagrams in the less-explored NIR, and to investigate the nature of the ionizing and heating source. We analyze the high-resolution spectra of the circum-nuclear regions of nine local (z < 0.1) U/LIRGS, investigating potential emission-line ratios to trace the excitation mechanisms acting on the line-emitting gas. We investigate these objects using the well-established [Fe ii]/PaB versus H2/Bry diagram, and attempt to correlate its classifications with other emission features across the spectrum. We then compare the empirical classifications with photo-ionization models, in order to evaluate how accurately the data can be reproduced. Finally, we compare the line width at 80% of the total flux (W80 ) of selected emission lines with the corresponding gas excitation mechanisms. We propose two line-excitation diagnostic diagrams based on [C i]/Pay and H2 1-0 O(5)/PAH 3.3 um ratio, which we found to directly correlate with the hardness of the radiation field, and therefore with the gas excitation mechanisms. In addition, the line-kinematics analysis shows that the W80 values of regions excited by star formation are on average slightly lower than those of AGN-excited regions, while shock-excited regions display distinctively higher W80 values compared to the other two groups. Our JWST-NIRSpec results reinforce previous studies showing that the H2 emission in the central regions of AGN hosts is complex and likely produced by multiple excitation mechanisms.

The authors propose two new NIR diagnostic diagrams ([C I]/Paγ vs. H₂ 1-0 O(5)/PAH 3.3 μm) that correlate with radiation field hardness, and show that W80 line widths differ between star formation, AGN, and shock-excited regions.
AI.motivation: Buried AGNs and obscured young stellar clusters challenge traditional optical diagnostic diagrams, necessitating new tools to trace excitation sources across the spectrum, particularly in the less-explored NIR regime.

title: A Compact Radio Ring with a Diffuse Envelope in LOFAR: Odd Radio Circle or Distinct Phenomenon?
comment: Submitted to A&A (16 pages)
summary: We report the discovery and investigate the nature of J1248+4826, an ORC-like source identified in the LOFAR Survey. We analyze its radio morphology, size, luminosity, and spectral properties, and study its environment and optical counterparts using multiwavelength data. We compare this source with other diffuse radio sources from the literature. J1248+4826 exhibits a well-defined ring of radius ~9" embedded in diffuse emission extending to ~1'. Assuming an association with a galaxy group at z=0.2, this corresponds to a physical radius of ~30 kpc, making it the most compact ORC candidate identified so far, while its total extent (~200 kpc), radio luminosity, and spectral index are consistent with the known ORC population. The putative host is the most massive group galaxy but it is located on the ring edge rather than in the center, unlike most known ORCs. We find no evidence for ongoing AGN activity, and both the morphology and spectral properties disfavor an origin as extended lobe from an active or dying radio galaxy, as well as fossil plasma re-accelerated by a virial shock. A more plausible scenario is that the source traces fossil plasma re-accelerated by shocks in the intragroup medium, possibly driven by galaxy interactions or mergers, although the compact ring size and high luminosity remain challenging to reproduce. If confirmed as an ORC, J1248+4826 would extend the population toward smaller physical scales and imply that compact systems may be underrepresented in current samples. The diffuse envelope further indicates that faint extended emission may be more common than previously recognized. This source highlights the diversity of diffuse radio sources and the likely role of group dynamics in shaping them, underscoring the need for larger samples, targeted follow-up observations and sophisticated simulations to discriminate between different formation scenarios.
